Most 'closet hacks' lists never say what anything costs or fits. I compared 6 small-closet organizers by price ($13.99-$179.99), size, and the exact problem each one solves. Here's what actually works.
Swapped every hanger on my rod for slim velvet ones ($39.99/set). Same rod, 15 more garments of space. 231,174 reviews at 4.8 stars later, I believe the hype.
$180 for a closet system sounds like a lot until you've bought rods, shelves, and drawers separately three times and still wasted the inches. Built-to-size beats piecemeal, every time.

$13.99 for 6 dorm organizers = $2.33 each. Material's thinner than a rigid bin that costs 4x more, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Still the cheapest way to test what your closet actually needs.
The most wasted space in a small closet isn't the floor — it's the foot of dead air above your rod. Fixed mine with a $22.49 no-drill floating shelf. Renters, this one's for you.
No closet in your apartment? A $35.99 freestanding rack with 7 hooks and 3 shelves is the only pick on my list that doesn't assume you have a closet frame to begin with.
Before you spend $180 on a closet system, try the $39.99 fix first: slim hangers. It won't fix a shelf problem, but if your rod is too full, this is step one.
I rated 6 closet organizers by price, size, and actual reviewer complaints — not by which one had the prettiest photo. $13.99 to $179.99, sorted by which small-space problem each one fixes.
A 5-foot reach-in closet and a 6-foot builder-grade closet need different fixes. Buying the same 'universal' kit for both is how you end up with wasted inches either way.
Corners of a closet are where things go to disappear. A $24.99 set of 4 lazy susan turntables (4.7 stars, 6,190 reviews) fixes that specific dead-zone problem — nothing else on my list does.
